# What stands in for a symbol alias reached through the standard library

Status: `open`, Crustify `06c62a2` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/std-symbol-alias-stand-ins`,
awaiting review.

## Signal

A rule an agent had to work out by hand that a skill should state. `porting-symbols`' Macros
section ports a symbol alias of an out-of-tree library's entity "as that entity's route reaches
it ...: through the standard library, it is a native function". `binding-symbols`' Macros
section puts a symbol alias's anchor on "the safe wrapper of the symbol it names", and the
record's row for `symbol-alias-anchors` on that symbol's stand-ins. An entity reached through the
standard library has no wrapper and no stand-in in the crate. No item of the standard library
can carry an anchor. And an alias of a type, or of the routine that releases one, is not a
function. So nothing said which item carries such a macro's anchor, nor what shape that item
takes.

## Evidence

`modules/libgit2/src/util/thread.c/wave-226/batch-2/run-1` ported 19 macros of
`src/util/unix/pthread.h`. Each names a POSIX entity. `git_mutex` is `pthread_mutex_t`, and
`git_mutex_init`, `_lock`, `_unlock` and `_free` are `pthread_mutex_init`, `_lock`, `_unlock` and
`_destroy`. The same holds for `git_cond`, `git_rwlock` and their operations, and
`git_thread_create` and `git_thread_join` are `pthread_create` and `pthread_join`. The header
keeps them for the C that remains, so their Rust forms are linked to no C, and they reach
`std::sync::Mutex`, `Condvar`, `RwLock` and `std::thread`. The run had to decide where 19
anchors go. A `pub type Mutex<T> = std::sync::Mutex<T>` could carry `mac::git_mutex`'s anchor,
but nothing could carry `git_mutex_lock`'s or `git_mutex_free`'s. So it wrote
`src/libgit2/src/util/thread.rs`'s `Mutex`, `Condvar` and `RwLock`, a newtype each over the
standard type, and `JoinHandle`, over `std::thread::JoinHandle`. Each operation macro is a method
(`Mutex::new`, `lock`, `MutexGuard::unlock`, `Condvar::wait`, `notify_one`, `RwLock::read`,
`write`, the guards' `unlock`), `git_thread_create` is the free function `spawn`, and each
`_free` is the type's `Drop::drop`, which `#[doc(alias)]` accepts on a trait impl's method.
`ffimap api` over the worklist keys all 19 as `new`, each with its stand-in.

## Goal

Consistency. The section already gives this case a pattern, "a native function", which does
not fit an alias of a type or of a release, so a run either leaves such a macro unanchored, as a
re-export of a standard item would, or shapes its stand-in its own way. Two such shapes cost a
consumer, who meets a different API for each header's locks, and a reviewer. The fitness
measure is the conventions findings per item; the change expects none on such a macro's anchor.
This is the case's first occurrence, so the proposal corrects the pattern the section gives
rather than adding one.

## Destination

The spec, `porting-symbols`' Macros section, which the translator evolves.

## Change

Crustify `06c62a2`: the section's last sentence becomes "through the standard library, it is a
native item of its module, which carries the alias's anchor, since no item of the standard
library can. An alias of a type is a type of the module over the standard one, an alias of an
operation on it that type's method, and an alias of the operation that releases it that type's
`Drop`."

## Validation

By the evidence that motivated it. The run above ported the 19 macros so. Its lints, with
warnings denied, accept the anchors on the three `Drop::drop` methods. Its `ffimap api` measure
finds every key of the worklist.

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per

# Porting symbols

How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust: the symbol route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s; the types it reaches are
[`porting-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s.

A ported symbol's implementation is translated to safe, idiomatic Rust with its observable
behaviour preserved.

## 1. Functions

A ported function takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Functions
section gives a function, or keeps its wrapper's, as [`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes.

A function no wrapper gives an API yet, whose body only reads or writes one member, or only
returns a value an existing item of its own module's safe API already gives, is ported as
that item, so that the port writes no second API: the accessor or method carries the
function's `Replaces` anchor and alias beside its own. Its export, where remaining C calls
it, is written in the module's gateway, over that item.

A function that remaining C calls or takes the address of is exported, as
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes. Its gateway undoes what the safe API converted,
so that its C callers see what the C function did: it rebuilds the safe arguments from the
C ones, writes the out-parameters and buffers through the pointers C passed, and reports a
failure through the function's C error convention, its return and the error state the C
function set, `errno` included, which the Rust behind it never sets. A panic is caught at
the gateway and reported as a failure, or aborts where the function cannot fail: none
unwinds into C. The gateway checks each export against the raw binding of the C declaration
it replaces, as [`testing-gates`](../../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions
section asks, in a constant the compiler evaluates, `const _: () = { let _ = [sys::<name>,
<name>]; };`, whose two function items coerce to one function-pointer type only where their
signatures agree; the binding is allowlisted for it where the bindings lack it. A variadic function's export cannot be defined on stable Rust, so a shim
keeps its C signature, as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, and calls
a fixed-arity export with the arguments it formats or unpacks. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the
export, with the raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it and its declaration in its
header, once no remaining C references it. C that only a configuration the target is built
without compiles, such as another platform's, is no remaining C: like a test case
configured out, as [`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Tests
follow their modules section describes, it holds no export back, and a build under that
configuration meets the function undeclared where it calls it.

A lifecycle routine's port reimplements it behind the policy its type's port or wrap
wrote, which it repoints at the Rust routine, and writes no API of its own, as `binding-types`'
Lifecycle section has the symbol route skip what a type batch emitted. The last of its
type's own module's memory users to be ported moves its storage to Rust's allocator,
unless C of other modules still allocates or frees it raw, which leaves that move to its
`port/memory`.

## 2. Globals

A ported global takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Globals section gives a global, or keeps its wrapper's. Rust holds its storage from its
port, beside its module's C, which keeps its own copy until the switch; from then on
the Rust's is the only one. A global that remaining C accesses
is exported, as a function is, and keeps the C layout and the synchronization protocol
those accesses rely on while it is. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the export, as
a function's does, and its storage then takes a native form, as state moved out of C does.
A thread-local one cannot be defined for C on stable Rust, so a shim keeps its C definition,
as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, until that stage. A global no
remaining C accesses is native from its port.

## 3. Function pointers

A ported function pointer keeps the safe callable type
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section gives it, which is its API from its port: its Rust consumers, and
the ported code that calls it, use that type alone. While remaining C calls a function
pointer of its type or supplies one, its C form stays beneath it: the function-pointer type
of its raw binding, the trampolines through which a Rust closure reaches the C that calls
it, and the `unsafe` constructor through which a C function reaches Rust, passed to an
export, whose gateway builds the C variant from the function and the context it receives,
or stored where C wrote it. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes that C form, with the
raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C references it, as
[`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section times it. A
function pointer no remaining C calls or supplies by its port is native in its
implementation too: its closure or trait alone.
A function pointer on the target's public API keeps its closure or trait through its
`port/unexport`, even when Rust alone implements it, so that the deferred public C API, as
[`conventions`](../../conventions/SKILL.md)'s Exports section describes, can let C
implement it again.

## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.
<!-- TODO: cross-language LTO (`-Clinker-plugin-lto`, with a clang whose LLVM matches
rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,
which reaches the Rust items its expansion uses once they are ported. A macro a TU defines
goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C
may expand, also stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported, and its C and Rust
forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration is ported once where every
configuration's expansion computes the same result for every input, and its documentation
names the branches the build does not take. Only one whose branches differ in what they
compute keeps the shim `binding-symbols` gives it: a port reimplements the body, and a shim
over the C's expansion would make it a binding. A symbol alias of an out-of-tree library's
entity is ported as that entity's route reaches it, as
[`dependencies`](../../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section checks it:
through the standard library, it is a native item of its module, which carries the alias's
anchor, since no item of the standard library can. An alias of a type is a type of the
module over the standard one, an alias of an operation on it that type's method, and an alias
of the operation that releases it that type's `Drop`.

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
....
A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.

The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search. An item whose
own name is that path, a name of the source the Rust keeps, carries no alias: rustdoc
rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers the search. Its
anchor is unchanged.

### 3.1 What is annotated

The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:

- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.

### 3.2 Several stand-ins

One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.

A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

## 1. Routes

What a campaign uses of an out-of-tree library is reached, in this order of preference:

1. through the Rust standard library, wherever no state is shared with C, as
   [Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes;
2. through established crates adopted for parts of the library, extended in a fork where
   they lack a little, as [Adopted crates](#6-adopted-crates) describes;
3. bound locally, in the consuming module's own `ffi_import` region over the library's
   established `-sys` crate, such as `libc`, for what is left too small to be worth a
   wrapper, as [Local bindings](#7-local-bindings) describes; and
4. through the library's crustify campaign, a wrap campaign of its own whose crate is the
   library's Crustify wrapper, as the rest of this section and
   [Side campaigns](#3-side-campaigns) describe.

The routes are named `std`, `crate`, `local` and `crustify-campaign` in
`dependencies.json`. The plan records each library's candidate crates, each with its
quality assessment, and maps every entity the campaign uses of the library to what each
candidate and the standard library offer for it, recommending a route for each entity and,
from those, the crates to adopt and the route of what they leave uncovered. Once the plan is
complete, the recommendation is put to the user, who chooses per library, and the choice
is recorded as the library's `decision`, as
[`dependencies-schema`](../../artifacts/dependencies-schema/SKILL.md) describes. The
records inform the choice; they do not make it. Each entity's route is then checked against
the code by the first batch that needs it, as [Confirmation](#8-confirmation) describes.

A library's wrapper is a wrap campaign of the source it is built from, in a repository of
its own: `<source>-crustify` under the `crustify-rs` organization, `<source>` being the
name of that source's repository, named and laid out as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section and [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s
Tree section describe for any wrap campaign, so that a later campaign whose target is the
source itself continues it. The libraries one source builds share its wrapper, each a link
unit of it: OpenSSL's `libcrypto` and `libssl` are both wrapped in `openssl-crustify`.
It is cloned beside the campaign's repository, as `../<source>-crustify`, never inside
it. The campaign's workspace depends on its crate by
Git, pinned to a commit, with a Cargo `[patch]` pointing at the clone while the campaign
extends it; the parent campaign's safe crate, its raw bindings included, names its safe
wrappers, never its raw bindings once a safe wrapper exists.

A wrapper covers only what the campaigns that use it reach through it: the entities
their waves need through the wrapper rather than the standard library, wrapped as those
waves need them. It exposes its own safe
types, with no conversions to or from the types of other crates that wrap the same
library.

## 2. Standard-library equivalents

The campaign's Rust reaches an out-of-tree library's entity through the Rust standard
library wherever the state the entity works on stays in Rust, or crosses to C only as
values the boundary converts, and through the library's wrapper wherever that state is
shared with C, as [`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section describes. The plan recommends which for each entity, from what it knows of the
uses; the batch that first needs the entity judges it from the code, as
[Confirmation](#8-confirmation) describes, so a wrapper covers what the campaign's Rust
reaches through it as its waves need it.

....
## 8. Confirmation

An entity's route is a recommendation made before any of its uses was translated. The first
batch that binds or ports one of its users checks the route against the code it translates,
by the uses the entity's `match` and note describe, and reports what it found in its final
message, which is recorded as the entity's `confirmation`. Each later batch takes
the confirmed route.

When the route does not hold, the batch reaches the entity through another route the
library's `decision` already allows, in this order: the standard library, where
[Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) allows it; another crate the
decision adopts for the library; the decision's `uncovered` route. A `crustify-campaign`
route that the library's crustify campaign does not yet cover is reported, and advanced as
[Side campaigns](#3-side-campaigns) describes, before the batch runs again. Where no route
the decision allows serves the entity, because the library leaves nothing `uncovered` or
only a crate the user has not adopted would, the batch reports it, and it is put
to the user, whose answer is recorded among the decision's `overrides`.

**Verdict: rejected.** The change needs two fixes before it lands. It does not weaken a check, and its rule uses none of libgit2's names.

I read the proposal on `wave-226` and the diff `57005de..06c62a2` under `libgit2-crustify/devel` (`57005de`). I checked the evidence against the landed `8aa231a69`: the `thread.rs` stand-ins, and the run's `api-diff.json`, which shows all 19 keys as `new` with none missing. As instructed, I ran no gate or rerun, created no scratch, and changed and landed nothing.

## Fixes required

1. **The rule doesn't match the evidence it rests on, so runs would produce two different shapes.** The new text says "an alias of an operation on it [is] that type's method". The run placed 5 of its 19 macros elsewhere:
   - `git_mutex_unlock`, `git_rwlock_rdunlock` and `git_rwlock_wrunlock` are methods of the guard types (`MutexGuard::unlock`, `RwLockReadGuard::unlock`, `RwLockWriteGuard::unlock`), not of the lock types.
   - `git_thread_create` is the free function `spawn`.
   - `git_thread_join` is `JoinHandle::join`. `JoinHandle` stands in for none of the aliased types; `git_thread` is a separate type with its own C form, `Thread`.

   A later run following the text literally would write `Mutex::unlock(guard)` or a `JoinHandle::spawn`. That is the second shape the proposal's consistency goal is meant to prevent. It also means the Validation line "The run above ported the 19 macros so" is not accurate. The fix is to state the shape the run actually used: each alias is anchored on the module's item that mirrors the standard item it reaches. That is a method of the module's type, or of the guard or handle the standard API returns, or a free function where the standard one is free. Then correct the Validation section, and the record row's change column if its wording changes.

2. **It contradicts the `conventions` anchor rules.** Section 3.1 says a macro's annotation goes on "the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it". The new rule puts macro anchors on:
   - a non-generic struct (`Condvar` carries `mac::git_cond`);
   - a trait impl's method (`Drop::drop` carries the `_free` macros), which a consumer never imports in place of the C item.

   A reviewer judging by `conventions` could file these anchors as misplaced, which is exactly the row's own recurrence signal. The fix is to extend 3.1's macro bullet in the same change so it covers the stand-ins `porting-symbols` gives an alias reached through the standard library. `conventions` is not a protected path.

## Checks that pass

- **Routes:** the rule agrees with `dependencies`' std route and its Confirmation section. No state is shared with C: the header keeps its macros for the remaining C, and no lock or thread crosses between the two.
- **Macros section:** it agrees with the rest of `porting-symbols`' Macros section, where the C and Rust forms are unlinked.
- **`binding-symbols`:** the change leaves its rule for an alias with a wrapper as it is.
- **Placement:** the change is in the right section, which is not a protected path.
- **Target's names:** the rule text has none. Its only non-generic name is Rust's `Drop`.
- **Record row:** it names a recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `watched` is the right status.
- **Prior row:** the proposal cites the `symbol-alias-anchors` row. That row has not recurred, since no review finding was filed.
- **Weakens a check:** no. No gate, lint, objective, test or tool detection changes, and `ffimap api` still keys every item.

## Not required

- **An empty `impl Drop` written only to carry an anchor costs the API.** Its dropck is stricter than `std::sync::Mutex`'s: a `Mutex<&'a T>` must now be dropped while `'a` is still live. It also blocks moving fields out. Putting the `_free` anchor on the type itself would avoid both.
- **"Symbol alias" now covers type aliases without saying so.** `binding-symbols` and `decomposition` use the term for aliases of a function or global.
- **The same anchor gap exists on the `crate` route,** since an adopted crate's items cannot carry anchors either. Leaving it for its own evidence is reasonable.
- **The proposal has no row yet in `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md` on `wave-226`.** That is the index writer's to add.
- **I could not verify, without a rerun, whether rustdoc search indexes an alias on a trait impl's method.** The run reports only that its lints accept it.

I proposed, changed and recorded nothing. The verdict is for the proposal's Review section, which the assistant records.
